SLC22A5 (commonly called OCTN2) belongs to the SLC22 family of solute carriers, a group of membrane transporters that includes organic cation (OCT), organic anion (OAT) and organic cation/carnitine (OCTN) subfamilies. Members of this family are typically 12-transmembrane-helix proteins that mediate facilitated or secondary-active transport of small organic molecules across plasma membranes. OCTN2 is the prototypical high-affinity, Na⁺-dependent carnitine transporter within the OCTN subfamily and is distinguished from its close relative OCTN1 (SLC22A4), which preferentially transports ergothioneine.1,2
In the brain, OCTN2 is expressed at the blood-brain barrier and in several brain cell types (including astrocytes and neurons), enabling regulated uptake of carnitine and some acylcarnitines into the central nervous system (CNS). Because the brain has limited capacity for long-chain fatty-acid β-oxidation compared with peripheral tissues, carnitine in the CNS is thought to support local energy metabolism, maintain acyl-group buffering (removing excess acyl-CoA by formation of acylcarnitines), and contribute to neurodevelopmental and neuroprotective processes. Studies of OCTN2 localization in brain show transporter presence in capillary endothelium and in perivascular astrocytic elements, supporting a role in trans-endothelial transport across the BBB and in astrocyte–neuron metabolic coupling. Impaired OCTN2 activity (systemic carnitine deficiency) can have neurological manifestations, reinforcing its functional importance in the brain.2,5,6
